XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Reform UK: Refferenda lleol ar gyfer codiadau'r dreth gyngor
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
For too many people across Wales, opening the annual council tax bill is something they absolutely dread. Families are struggling with the cost of living. They're working hard to pay their mortgages whilst grappling with energy bills and weekly shopping, yet they're also being asked to find more and more money every year to pay their council tax. In my constituency of Caerdydd Ffynnon Taf, a standard band D bill in Cardiff has risen from around £1,637 in 2022-23 to over £2,000 this year—an increase of almost 23 per cent. And it's not just my constituency. Let us look at the figures elsewhere. In 2025-26, Wrexham and Flintshire increased council tax by 9.5 per cent, Pembrokeshire by 9.35 per cent and Ceredigion by 9.3 per cent. In Conwy, residents have faced successive increases of 9.67 per cent, 8.95 per cent and a further 6.5 per cent this year. And on Ynys Môn, the council's band D charge has risen more than 31 per cent since 2022. On average, that's over £425 more each year added to their council tax bill. Staggering. Yet, the Plaid Cymru-led council on Ynys Môn reported a budget underspend, totalling over £8 million across the last three financial years, and holds £19 million in general reserves. Surely, it is reasonable to ask whether residents were charged more than was necessary.

It isn't just about the money they haven't spent. It's also about the stupid decisions they've committed to spend on. A few weeks ago, the Isle of Anglesey County Council passed a motion to spend £1.1 million swapping household black bins for smaller ones. Only one councillor voted against that proposal, and I am proud to say that that was a sole Reform Cymru councillor—[Interruption.] There'll be more than one soon. A lonely voice of common sense in a crowded room of nonsense. Let me be clear, of course councils face genuine pressures, from social care to schools, roads and waste collection—these all need funding. We understand that and we want to see them fairly funded, but that does not mean that ever-higher council tax bills should be accepted as the norm. Wales has 22 principal local authorities, so let me ask a straightforward question: do we really need 22 separate back offices when councils could work together to save money? Do we need duplicated payroll systems, separate IT contracts and independent procurement arrangements when sharing services could deliver better value? Could councils combine their purchasing power to secure better prices, reduce duplication and free up money for front-line services, such as social care? This is not an attack on local government employees. They are common-sense questions about the political leadership of Welsh councils.

Greater efficiency is one reason Reform wants to introduce a democratic lock on annual council tax increases above 4.99 per cent. We see this policy working as an active deterrent against wasteful and unnecessary spending. If Welsh councils want to raise tax above this threshold, they must make a convincing case through a local referendum. It is up to local people to decide whether their money is being spent efficiently. Consider a household paying £2,000 a year in council tax. A 4.99 per cent increase would add £100 to its bill and an 8 per cent increase would add £160. During a cost-of-living crisis, every pound matters. In England, councils are generally required to seek approval through a local referendum if they want to increase council tax beyond the relevant threshold. So, why shouldn't Welsh taxpayers have the same democratic safeguard? Our objective isn't to force councils to make indiscriminate cuts or undermine essential services, it is to challenge unnecessary duplication, improve procurement, review administrative overheads and encourage councils to work together, wherever that delivers savings.

We would also expect greater transparency so that residents can see how their money is spent, what savings have been achieved and why any proposed council tax increase above the threshold is necessary. The people of Wales work hard for their money. They deserve responsible spending, effective services and a fair deal from local government. The answer to every budget pressure cannot simply be another inflation-busting increase in council tax. Plaid Cymru talk about a new deal for Wales, but what the people of Wales really need is a fair deal from all layers of Government within Wales. It's time for the Welsh Government to set the bar.

But I know what will happen. Like every other major issue in Wales, Plaid will say it's somebody else's job to fix, someone else's responsibility. 'Council tax is a local matter for councils.' We've heard it before. This is where Reform is different. We will stand up for Wales and fight the corner of local people. We will make sure their voices are heard loud and clear. We will set the standard, and in this case, that means giving taxpayers the final say on high council tax increases. If Members here today want to help people with the cost of living, put your money where your mouth is and back this democratic lock. Their money, their decision.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
I ormod o bobl ledled Cymru, mae bil blynyddol y dreth gyngor yn rhywbeth y maent yn arswydo rhagddo. Mae teuluoedd yn ei chael hi'n anodd ymdopi â chostau byw. Maent yn gweithio'n galed i dalu eu morgeisi gan ymgodymu â biliau ynni a siopa wythnosol, ond mae disgwyl iddynt ddod o hyd i fwy a mwy o arian bob blwyddyn i dalu'r dreth gyngor hefyd. Yn fy etholaeth i, Caerdydd Ffynnon Taf, mae bil safonol band D yng Nghaerdydd wedi codi o oddeutu £1,637 yn 2022-23 i dros £2,000 eleni—cynnydd o bron i 23 y cant. Ac nid yn fy etholaeth i yn unig y mae hyn yn digwydd. Gadewch inni edrych ar y ffigurau mewn mannau eraill. Yn 2025-26, cynyddodd Wrecsam a sir y Fflint y dreth gyngor 9.5 y cant, sir Benfro 9.35 y cant a Cheredigion 9.3 y cant. Yng Nghonwy, mae trigolion wedi wynebu codiadau olynol o 9.67 y cant, 8.95 y cant a 6.5 y cant pellach eleni. Ac ar Ynys Môn, mae bil band D y cyngor wedi codi fwy na 31 y cant ers 2022. Ar gyfartaledd, mae hynny dros £425 yn fwy bob blwyddyn wedi'i ychwanegu at fil y dreth gyngor. Syfrdanol. Ac eto, adroddodd y cyngor a arweinir gan Blaid Cymru ar Ynys Môn danwariant yn eu cyllideb, cyfanswm o dros £8 miliwn dros y tair blynedd ariannol ddiwethaf, ac mae ganddynt £19 miliwn mewn cronfeydd wrth gefn cyffredinol. Mae'n rhesymol gofyn a godwyd mwy nag oedd angen ar drigolion.

Mae a wnelo hyn â mwy na'r arian nad ydynt wedi'i wario yn unig. Mae a wnelo hefyd â'r penderfyniadau gwirion y maent wedi ymrwymo i wario arnynt. Ychydig wythnosau yn ôl, derbyniodd Cyngor Sir Ynys Môn gynnig i wario £1.1 miliwn ar gyfnewid biniau duon cartrefi am rai llai. Dim ond un cynghorydd a bleidleisiodd yn erbyn y cynnig hwnnw, ac rwy'n falch o ddweud mai cynghorydd o Reform Cymru oedd hwnnw—[Torri ar draws.] Bydd mwy nag un cyn bo hir. Un llais dros synnwyr cyffredin mewn ystafell yn orlawn o nonsens. Gadewch imi fod yn glir, wrth gwrs bod cynghorau'n wynebu pwysau gwirioneddol, o ofal cymdeithasol i ysgolion, ffyrdd a chasglu gwastraff—mae angen cyllid ar y rhain i gyd. Rydym yn deall hynny ac rydym am eu gweld yn cael eu hariannu'n deg, ond nid yw hynny'n golygu y dylid derbyn biliau treth gyngor sy'n cynyddu'n dragywydd fel y norm. Mae gan Gymru 22 o brif awdurdodau lleol, felly gadewch imi ofyn cwestiwn syml: a oes angen 22 o swyddfeydd cefn gwahanol arnom pan allai cynghorau gydweithio i arbed arian? A oes angen dyblygu systemau cyflogres, contractau TG gwahanol a threfniadau caffael annibynnol arnom pan allai rhannu gwasanaethau ddarparu gwerth gwell? A allai cynghorau gyfuno eu pŵer prynu i sicrhau prisiau gwell, lleihau dyblygu a rhyddhau arian ar gyfer gwasanaethau rheng flaen, fel gofal cymdeithasol? Nid ymosodiad ar weithwyr llywodraeth leol mo hwn. Maent yn gwestiynau synnwyr cyffredin ynglŷn ag arweinyddiaeth wleidyddol cynghorau Cymru.

Mae mwy o arbedion effeithlonrwydd yn un rheswm pam y mae Reform eisiau cyflwyno clo democrataidd ar godiadau blynyddol uwchlaw 4.99 y cant i'r dreth gyngor. Rydym yn gweld y polisi hwn yn gweithio i atal gwariant gwastraffus a diangen. Os yw cynghorau Cymru eisiau codi treth uwchlaw'r trothwy hwn, rhaid iddynt wneud achos argyhoeddiadol drwy refferendwm lleol. Mater i bobl leol yw penderfynu a yw eu harian yn cael ei wario'n effeithlon. Ystyriwch aelwyd sy'n talu £2,000 y flwyddyn drwy'r dreth gyngor. Byddai cynnydd o 4.99 y cant yn ychwanegu £100 at eu bil, a byddai cynnydd o 8 y cant yn ychwanegu £160. Mewn argyfwng costau byw, mae pob punt yn bwysig. Yn Lloegr, yn gyffredinol mae'n ofynnol i gynghorau geisio cymeradwyaeth drwy refferendwm lleol os ydynt eisiau cynyddu'r dreth gyngor y tu hwnt i'r trothwy perthnasol. Felly, pam na ddylai trethdalwyr Cymru gael yr un mesur diogelwch democrataidd? Nid ein hamcan yw gorfodi cynghorau i wneud toriadau diwahân neu danseilio gwasanaethau hanfodol, ond yn hytrach, herio dyblygu diangen, gwella caffael, adolygu costau gweinyddol ac annog cynghorau i gydweithio, lle bynnag y bydd hynny'n cyflawni arbedion.

Byddem hefyd yn disgwyl mwy o dryloywder fel y gall trigolion weld sut y mae eu harian yn cael ei wario, pa arbedion a gyflawnwyd a pham y bydd unrhyw gynnydd arfaethedig yn y dreth gyngor uwchlaw'r trothwy yn angenrheidiol. Mae pobl Cymru’n gweithio'n galed am eu harian. Maent yn haeddu gwariant cyfrifol, gwasanaethau effeithiol a bargen deg gan lywodraeth leol. Ni all yr ateb i unrhyw bwysau cyllidebol fod yn gynnydd arall uwch na chwyddiant yn y dreth gyngor. Mae Plaid Cymru yn sôn am fargen newydd i Gymru, ond yr hyn sydd ei angen ar bobl Cymru mewn gwirionedd yw bargen deg gan bob haen o Lywodraeth yng Nghymru. Mae'n bryd i Lywodraeth Cymru osod y safon.

Ond rwy'n gwybod beth fydd yn digwydd. Fel pob mater pwysig arall yng Nghymru, bydd Plaid Cymru yn dweud mai gwaith rhywun arall yw mynd i'r afael ag ef, cyfrifoldeb rhywun arall. 'Mae'r dreth gyngor yn fater lleol i gynghorau.' Rydym wedi'i glywed o'r blaen. Dyma ble mae Reform yn wahanol. Byddwn yn sefyll dros Gymru ac yn ymladd dros bobl leol. Byddwn yn sicrhau bod eu lleisiau'n cael eu clywed yn glir ac yn uchel. Byddwn yn gosod y safon, ac yn yr achos hwn, mae hynny'n golygu rhoi'r gair olaf i drethdalwyr ar godiadau mawr yn y dreth gyngor. Os yw'r Aelodau yma heddiw eisiau helpu pobl gyda chostau byw, rhowch eich arian ar eich gair a chefnogwch y clo democrataidd hwn. Eu harian nhw, eu penderfyniad nhw.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Reform UK: Refferenda lleol ar gyfer codiadau'r dreth gyngor
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
I want to address why referendums on council tax increases above 4.99 per cent would be utterly unfeasible. Now, I'm not going to get into a debate about whether we should be lowering council tax or not. I'm going to be looking at the practical aspects of whether a referendum would work or not. So, before I start, let's be honest, Reform UK Wales is what you name yourself, not Reform Cymru. Reform Cymru does not exist.

Anyway, in 13 years, across over 300 English authorities, one referendum has been held: Bedfordshire's police and crime commissioner in 2015. It failed. In England, council taxes can be increased without holding a referendum, and that power has been used regularly. If a mechanism designed to trigger local votes produces no local votes, it is not facilitating local democratic choice.

What a referendum does is two things. The first is a ceiling becomes a floor. A council that might have raised council tax by 2 per cent or 3 per cent in an easier year raises it by the maximum every year because the cap compounds. Forgone revenue cannot be recovered later, so the rational response is to build up the reserves that you have and to take the maximum annually and build a buffer. The second is where that cap bites: services are cut rather than referendums held. Birmingham, Nottingham, Croydon, Thurrock and Woking have all issued section 114 notices in recent years, effective local bankruptcy in a system with referendums and still no referendums. It is clear that even though this mechanism exists in practice in England, it is either barely used or superseded because circumstances are so dire.

So, let me turn to why this would operate differently and worse in Wales. A referendum costs a local authority somewhere between £150,000 and £600,000 to run. That is not a large sum against the total budget, but the total budget is the wrong denominator. Between 80 per cent to 85 per cent of a council's spending is committed to statutory duties, teacher salaries, statutory social care, waste collection, additional learning needs. We all know that these need to be accounted and budgeted for. A referendum cannot be taken from those. It comes from discretionary services or from unallocated reserves.

For Cardiff, I'll admit that is absorbable within central contingencies, but for Merthyr Tydfil, a £300,000 cost represents a materially different proportion of unallocated general reserves. In some Welsh authorities, that is between 5 per cent and 7 per cent of the entire safety net in a single hit. In service terms, that is a library, youth provision or a year of community transport. The motion sends it to Merthyr, it doesn't send it to Cardiff.

Then there is the tax-based vulnerability, which this motion appears not to have considered at all. In wealthy English shire counties, a 4.99 per cent rise generates substantial revenue, because a high proportion of properties sit in bands E to I. In Welsh Valleys and much of rural Wales, over 70 per cent of properties sit in bands A to C. The same percentage rise yields a fraction of the revenue. This means a lower income authority must raise it by a higher percentage simply to generate the same money. It is therefore pushed towards a referendum threshold, precisely because the tax base is so weak, and we know that of Wales. So, the authorities most likely to be forced into a referendum are the ones least able to afford to be. It's not Cardiff, it's not the wealthy English shires, it's Blaenau Gwent and Merthyr Tydfil, and they would spend a significant fraction of the additional yield on the ballot itself. And then there is the risk of losing it, which is not a small risk, and that would mean that libraries would shut, youth provisions would go and community transport would be axed. Stand-alone referendums outside of a general election cycle typically see turnout of between 15 per cent to 25 per cent. A referendum on a single percentage figure for council tax would certainly fall below that: you're looking at 5 per cent to 10 per cent. There is no candidate, no campaign, no competing vision, simply a number put to the public on a Thursday in February. And the motivational asymmetry is severe: a resident angry about a tax rise will turn out to vote 'no'; a resident who accepts that social care and libraries need funding rarely feels strong enough to turn out for 'yes'. The result is not a referendum on the budget; it is a referendum amongst the people most opposed to it.

There is a serious debate to be had about council tax and the funding settlement and about the burden on households. This is not this debate. In England, this policy produced one referendum in 13 years, a queue of bankrupt councils—Reform have looked at that and decided Wales should have some more.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Hoffwn fynd i'r afael â pham y byddai refferenda ar godiadau uwch na 4.99 y cant yn y dreth gyngor yn gwbl anymarferol. Nawr, nid wyf am ddechrau dadlau a ddylem ostwng y dreth gyngor ai peidio. Rwy'n mynd i edrych ar yr agweddau ymarferol o ran gweld a fyddai refferendwm yn gweithio ai peidio. Felly, cyn imi ddechrau, gadewch inni fod yn onest, Reform UK Wales yw'r hyn rydych chi'n galw eich hunain, nid Reform Cymru. Nid yw Reform Cymru yn bodoli.

Beth bynnag, mewn 13 mlynedd, ar draws dros 300 o awdurdodau Lloegr, un refferendwm a gynhaliwyd: comisiynydd heddlu a throseddu swydd Bedford yn 2015. Fe fethodd. Yn Lloegr, gellir cynyddu'r dreth gyngor heb gynnal refferendwm, ac mae'r pŵer hwnnw wedi cael ei ddefnyddio'n rheolaidd. Os nad yw mecanwaith a gynlluniwyd i sbarduno refferenda lleol yn cynhyrchu unrhyw bleidleisiau lleol, nid yw'n hwyluso dewis democrataidd lleol.

Mae refferendwm yn gwneud dau beth. Y cyntaf yw bod terfyn uchaf yn dod yn derfyn isaf. Mae cyngor a allai fod wedi codi'r dreth gyngor 2 y cant neu 3 y cant mewn blwyddyn haws yn ei chodi'n unol â'r uchafswm bob blwyddyn gan fod y cap yn compowndio. Ni ellir adennill refeniw a gollwyd yn nes ymlaen, felly'r ymateb rhesymegol yw gadael i'r cronfeydd wrth gefn sydd gennych gronni, codi'r uchafswm bob blwyddyn ac adeiladu clustog. Yr ail yw lle mae'r cap hwnnw'n brathu: mae gwasanaethau'n cael eu torri yn hytrach na bod refferenda'n cael eu cynnal. Mae Birmingham, Nottingham, Croydon, Thurrock a Woking oll wedi cyhoeddi hysbysiadau adran 114 yn y blynyddoedd diwethaf, methdaliad lleol i bob pwrpas mewn system gyda refferenda, ac eto, dim refferenda. Er bod y mecanwaith hwn yn bodoli yn ymarferol yn Lloegr, mae'n amlwg na wneir fawr o ddefnydd ohono o gwbl neu ei fod yn amherthnasol am fod yr amgylchiadau mor wael.

Felly, gadewch imi droi at pam y byddai hyn yn gweithredu'n wahanol ac yn waeth yng Nghymru. Mae'n costio rhwng £150,000 a £600,000 i awdurdod lleol gynnal refferendwm. Nid yw hynny'n swm mawr yn erbyn y gyllideb gyfan, ond nid y gyllideb gyfan yw'r enwadur cywir. Mae rhwng 80 y cant ac 85 y cant o wariant cyngor wedi'i glustnodi ar gyfer dyletswyddau statudol, cyflogau athrawon, gofal cymdeithasol statudol, casglu gwastraff, anghenion dysgu ychwanegol. Gŵyr pob un ohonom fod angen cyfrif am y rhain a'u cyllidebu. Ni ellir ariannu refferendwm o'r arian hwnnw. Mae'n dod o wasanaethau dewisol neu o gronfeydd wrth gefn heb eu dyrannu.

Yng Nghaerdydd, rwy'n cyfaddef y gellid talu am hynny drwy gronfeydd wrth gefn canolog, ond i Ferthyr Tudful, mae cost o £300,000 yn cynrychioli cyfran gwbl wahanol o gronfeydd wrth gefn cyffredinol heb eu dyrannu. Mewn rhai awdurdodau yng Nghymru, mae hynny'n cyfateb i rhwng 5 y cant a 7 y cant o'r rhwyd ddiogelwch gyfan mewn un ergyd. Yn nhermau gwasanaethau, mae hynny'n golygu llyfrgell, darpariaeth ieuenctid neu flwyddyn o drafnidiaeth gymunedol. Mae'r cynnig yn ei anfon i Ferthyr Tudful, nid yw'n ei anfon i Gaerdydd.

Wedyn, mae gennych fregusrwydd o ran y dreth ei hun nad yw'r cynnig hwn wedi'i ystyried o gwbl yn ôl pob golwg. Mewn siroedd cyfoethog yn Lloegr, mae cynnydd o 4.99 y cant yn cynhyrchu refeniw sylweddol, gan fod cyfran uchel o eiddo ym mandiau E i I. Yng Nghymoedd y De a llawer o gefn gwlad Cymru, mae dros 70 y cant o eiddo ym mandiau A i C. Mae'r un cynnydd canrannol yn cynhyrchu llawer llai o refeniw. Golyga hyn fod yn rhaid i awdurdod incwm is godi'r dreth ar ganran uwch i gynhyrchu'r un faint o arian. Felly, fe gaiff ei wthio tuag at drothwy refferendwm am fod y sylfaen dreth mor wan, a gwyddom hynny am Gymru. Felly, yr awdurdodau sydd fwyaf tebygol o gael eu gorfodi i gynnal refferendwm yw'r rhai sydd â'r lleiaf o allu i fforddio gwneud hynny. Nid Caerdydd, nid siroedd cyfoethog Lloegr, ond Blaenau Gwent a Merthyr Tudful, a byddent yn gwario cyfran sylweddol o'r incwm ychwanegol ar y bleidlais ei hun. Ac mae risg o golli, nad yw'n risg fach, a byddai hynny'n golygu y byddai llyfrgelloedd yn cau, y byddai darpariaethau ieuenctid yn diflannu ac y byddai trafnidiaeth gymunedol yn cael ei thorri. Canran o rhwng 15 y cant a 25 y cant sydd fel arfer yn pleidleisio mewn refferenda annibynnol y tu allan i gylch etholiad cyffredinol. Byddai refferendwm ar un ffigur canrannol ar gyfer y dreth gyngor yn sicr yn llai na hynny: rydych chi'n edrych ar 5 y cant i 10 y cant. Nid oes ymgeisydd, dim ymgyrch, dim gweledigaeth sy'n cystadlu, dim ond ffigur a roddir i'r cyhoedd ar ddydd Iau ym mis Chwefror. Ac mae'r anghymesuredd cymhellol yn ddifrifol: bydd preswylydd sy'n flin am gynnydd yn y dreth yn pleidleisio 'na'; anaml y bydd preswylydd sy'n derbyn bod angen cyllid ar ofal cymdeithasol a llyfrgelloedd yn teimlo'n ddigon cryf i bleidleisio o blaid. O ganlyniad, nid refferendwm ar y gyllideb a geir, ond refferendwm ymhlith y bobl sy'n ei gwrthwynebu fwyaf.

Mae dadl ddifrifol i'w chael ynglŷn â'r dreth gyngor a'r setliad cyllido ac ynglŷn â'r baich ar aelwydydd. Nid dyna yw'r ddadl hon. Yng Nghymru, mae'r polisi hwn wedi cynhyrchu un refferendwm mewn 13 mlynedd, ciw o gynghorau'n mynd yn fethdalwyr—mae Reform wedi edrych ar hynny a phenderfynu bod angen mwy o hyn ar Gymru.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Reform UK: Refferenda lleol ar gyfer codiadau'r dreth gyngor
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
I'm pleased to support the motion tabled by my colleague Llŷr Powell, but I want to approach it from a slightly different angle, because I've been a town councillor myself, and know something about setting budgets and council tax precepts.

I know it's not always easy; the constituency I represent covers parts of four council areas—Gwynedd, Wrexham, Powys and Denbighshire—and each faces its own challenges. But there's one thing they all have in common: every year, people receive their council tax bill and almost without fail it's gone up again. For someone on a good income, another £100 or £150 might not seem particularly significant, but, for a pensioner or someone living on a fixed income, that's money they've got to find from somewhere, and the trouble is that these increases don't happen in isolation; they build up year after year. A 5 per cent increase this year is added to all the increases that have gone before it, and next year's increase is calculated on top of that. That's why I think we need to look at what people are paying today compared with five or 10 years ago, rather than just looking at the latest percentage, because household incomes certainly haven't kept pace.

Now, having been a town councillor, there's something else I think that's worth explaining. When your council tax bill arrives, you might reasonably assume all that money is going to your county council, but it isn't. Part of it goes towards policing, and, depending on where you live, there's also a contribution to your town or community council. Fire and rescue services are funded through council budgets too. In fact, the police element alone accounts for roughly £1 in every £6 on the average council tax bill in Wales, and that's not an amount your county council decides. I mention this because I think people deserve to know exactly who is responsible for the different parts of their bill, and, if we're going to introduce a referendum threshold, we need to be clear about which increase it applies to.

Now, I don't want anyone to think I'm suggesting councils have an easy job; they don't. Social care costs are rising, schools are under pressure, and councils are being asked to deliver services with increasingly stretched budgets. But that brings me to something else that matters. Is the way we fund local government in Wales actually fit for purpose? Because delivering services in large rural counties like Powys, Gwynedd and Denbighshire is very different from delivering them in a city. You've got smaller communities spread over much greater distances. School transport costs more, providing services costs more, and, in many cases, there simply aren't the economies of scale that larger urban areas can achieve. So, we need a funding system that recognises those differences, not a one-size-fits-all approach that assumes every council faces the same circumstances.

The Welsh Government has a responsibility to get that right, because, if we're going to hold councils accountable for the money they ask residents to pay, we must also hold the Welsh Government accountable for the funding decisions that affect them. None of this changes the position of the person who has to pay the bill—they don't get to choose whether their income goes up enough to cover another council tax increase, they just have to find the money, and that's why I support giving them a greater say when particularly large increases are proposed. It doesn't mean councils can never put council tax up by more than 4.99 per cent; it means that, if they believe they need to, they should be prepared to explain why and put that decision to the people who are going to pay for it. I don't think that is unreasonable, because, ultimately, this isn't about figures on a spreadsheet or arguments between politicians, it's about what people have left in their pockets at the end of the month, and I think those people deserve a say. So, I'll be supporting this motion and urge other Members to do the same. Diolch, Lywydd.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Rwy'n falch o gefnogi'r cynnig a gyflwynwyd gan fy nghyd-Aelod Llŷr Powell, ond rwyf am fynd i'r afael ag ef o ongl ychydig yn wahanol, oherwydd rwyf wedi bod yn gynghorydd tref fy hun, ac yn gwybod rhywbeth am osod cyllidebau a praeseptau treth gyngor.

Rwy'n gwybod nad yw bob amser yn hawdd; mae'r etholaeth rwy'n ei chynrychioli yn cwmpasu rhannau o bedair ardal cyngor—Gwynedd, Wrecsam, Powys a sir Ddinbych—ac mae pob un yn wynebu ei heriau ei hun. Ond mae un peth ganddynt i gyd yn gyffredin: bob blwyddyn, mae pobl yn cael eu bil treth gyngor a bron bob tro mae wedi codi eto. I rywun ar incwm da, efallai na fydd £100 neu £150 arall yn ymddangos yn arbennig o arwyddocaol, ond i bensiynwr neu rywun sy'n byw ar incwm sefydlog, mae'n arian y mae'n rhaid iddynt ddod o hyd iddo o rywle, a'r broblem yw nad unwaith y mae'r codiadau hyn yn digwydd; maent yn cronni flwyddyn ar ôl blwyddyn. Mae cynnydd o 5 y cant eleni yn cael ei ychwanegu at yr holl godiadau sydd wedi mynd o'r blaen, ac mae cynnydd y flwyddyn nesaf yn cael ei gyfrifo ar ben hynny. Dyna pam y credaf fod angen inni edrych ar yr hyn y mae pobl yn ei dalu heddiw o'i gymharu â phum neu 10 mlynedd yn ôl, yn hytrach na dim ond edrych ar y ganran ddiweddaraf, oherwydd yn sicr, nid yw incwm cartrefi wedi codi ar yr un cyflymder.

Nawr, ar ôl bod yn gynghorydd tref, mae yna rywbeth arall y credaf ei fod yn werth ei esbonio. Pan fydd eich bil treth gyngor yn cyrraedd, efallai y byddwch chi'n cymryd yn ganiataol yn ddigon rhesymol fod yr holl arian hwnnw'n mynd i'ch cyngor sir, ond nid yw hynny'n wir. Mae rhan ohono'n mynd tuag at blismona, ac yn dibynnu ar ble rydych chi'n byw, mae yna gyfraniad i'ch cyngor tref neu gymuned hefyd. Mae gwasanaethau tân ac achub yn cael eu hariannu trwy gyllidebau'r cyngor hefyd. Mewn gwirionedd, mae'r elfen heddlu'n unig yn £1 ym mhob £6 ar gyfartaledd ym mil y dreth gyngor yng Nghymru, ac nid swm y mae eich cyngor sir yn ei benderfynu yw hwnnw. Rwy'n sôn am hyn am fy mod yn credu bod pobl yn haeddu gwybod yn union pwy sy'n gyfrifol am y gwahanol rannau o'u bil, ac os ydym yn mynd i gyflwyno trothwy refferendwm, mae angen inni fod yn glir pa gynnydd y mae'n berthnasol iddo.

Nawr, nid wyf eisiau i unrhyw un feddwl fy mod i'n awgrymu bod gan gynghorau waith hawdd; nid yw hynny'n wir. Mae costau gofal cymdeithasol yn codi, mae ysgolion dan bwysau, a gofynnir i gynghorau ddarparu gwasanaethau gyda chyllidebau dan bwysau cynyddol. Ond daw hynny â mi at rywbeth arall sy'n bwysig. A yw'r ffordd yr ariannwn lywodraeth leol yng Nghymru yn addas i'r diben mewn gwirionedd? Oherwydd mae darparu gwasanaethau mewn siroedd gwledig mawr fel Powys, Gwynedd a sir Ddinbych yn wahanol iawn i'w darparu mewn dinas. Mae gennych gymunedau llai wedi'u gwasgaru dros bellteroedd llawer mwy. Mae cludiant ysgol yn costio mwy, mae darparu gwasanaethau'n costio mwy, ac mewn llawer o achosion, ni cheir yr arbedion maint y gall ardaloedd trefol mwy eu cyflawni. Felly, mae angen system ariannu sy'n cydnabod y gwahaniaethau hynny, nid dull un maint i bawb sy'n cymryd yn ganiataol fod pob cyngor yn wynebu'r un amgylchiadau.

Mae gan Lywodraeth Cymru gyfrifoldeb i wneud hynny'n iawn, oherwydd, os ydym yn mynd i ddwyn cynghorau i gyfrif am yr arian y maent yn gofyn i drigolion ei dalu, rhaid inni hefyd ddwyn Llywodraeth Cymru i gyfrif am y penderfyniadau cyllido sy'n effeithio arnynt. Nid oes dim o hyn yn newid sefyllfa'r unigolyn sy'n gorfod talu'r bil—ni chânt ddewis a yw eu hincwm yn codi digon i dalu cynnydd arall yn y dreth gyngor, dim ond dod o hyd i'r arian, a dyna pam rwy'n cefnogi rhoi mwy o lais iddynt pan argymhellir cynnydd arbennig o fawr. Nid yw'n golygu na all cynghorau byth godi treth gyngor fwy na 4.99 y cant; mae'n golygu, os credant fod angen iddynt wneud hynny, y dylent fod yn barod i esbonio pam a rhoi'r penderfyniad hwnnw i'r bobl sy'n mynd i dalu amdano. Nid wyf yn credu bod hynny'n afresymol, oherwydd, yn y pen draw, nid mater o ffigurau ar daenlen neu ddadleuon rhwng gwleidyddion yw hyn, ond mater o'r hyn sydd gan bobl ar ôl yn eu pocedi ar ddiwedd y mis, ac rwy'n credu bod y bobl hynny'n haeddu cael lleisio barn. Felly, fe fyddaf yn cefnogi'r cynnig hwn ac yn annog yr Aelodau eraill i wneud yr un peth. Diolch, Lywydd.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
I've never heard people speak in a debate with so much ignorance. I will just respond to one thing. There's the Welsh purchasing consortium, where local authorities get together to buy things cheaply between themselves.

Local government provides many of the key services provided by the public sector in Wales—not just refuse collection, but hundreds of services, from road maintenance to trading standards. No local authority makes increases in council tax because they want to punish their electorate—that would be perverse and self-defeating. Council tax rises are driven by the need to meet demand, meet their statutory obligations and council tax payers' wishes. We must consider that budgetary pressures on local authorities are not a simplistic mathematical exercise. Why 4.99 per cent? I know it makes a good headline. Can Reform publish the calculations behind it? Which services would they consider scrapping? Are they seeking statutory services to be made non-statutory in order for councils to legally stop services? In Reform-led Kent, the budget financial risk register reveals an immediate exposure of £411 million—that's it, £411 million—indicating the scale of uncertainty facing Kent's finances. Risks include potential overspends, underfunded services, the pressure of increasing demand in social care, and infrastructure upkeep. This level of risk raises a question about the council's ability to manage its reserves and avoid more drastic cuts in coming years, gambling with services for the vulnerable and the council's finances.

The previous Senedd's Finance Committee received evidence from witnesses about the differential rates at which inflation affects and has an impact on their budgets. Local government in Wales has many financial pressures outside of its control. Education is a major area of expenditure and teachers' pay and pension increases need to be met in full. Education is the key to moving children out of poverty.

I want to discuss three major financial pressures on local government in detail. The estimated pressure for local government services for this year was £599 million. Social services alone account for almost half of that, equating to over £200 million all told. The provision of social care is critical to the health and care system operating effectively, and plays a key role in achieving positive health outcomes. Investing in social care leads directly to reducing pressure on the NHS, both in terms of keeping people out of hospital and helping people to return home at the appropriate time, reducing delayed transfers of care.

Wales has an ageing population and people are living for longer with complex care needs and dementia. This will continue to increase pressure on care services. The Welsh Local Government Association stress that social services face acute and widening financial challenges, with more than 81,000 people relying on care and support. Care Forum Wales says the sector is under immense strain, grappling with persistent workforce pressures, unsustainable fee rates and increasing employer costs. A committee was shown that fees for nursing care can vary by as much as £9,000 a year between neighbouring authorities. For those who fully fund their own care, so-called 'self-funders', average weekly costs are around £1,156 for residential care and £1,394 for nursing care. The older people's commissioner highlights how funding pressures fall unfairly on service users, with inequitable fee structures and top-up fees leaving many self-funders effectively subsidising publicly funded care home placements.

Workforce pressures: staffing pressures remain a major concern, with chronic vacancies and ongoing recruitment and retention difficulties, despite the introduction of the real living wage for social care workers. More than a quarter of domiciliary care workers are on zero-hours contracts. Social Care Wales's workforce survey in 2025 found that one in five social care employees aim to leave the sector within the next 14 months, citing low pay, poor conditions and limited progression.

The Welsh Government does not currently publish data on waiting times for social care services, but stakeholders report long and growing delays, including waits for assessment for care packages, equipment and occupational therapy. Age Cymru research found that nearly one in four older people were waiting more than 30 days for a care assessment and one in six were waiting more than 30 days for care to be put in place after the assessment.

Another major area of pressure is additional learning needs. We've talked about it a lot here, and everybody was saying how we need more money for additional learning needs. Where do you think it's going to come from? Schools across Wales are at breaking point. A significant number of school budgets are currently in deficit, and, for many, that crisis is driven almost directly—[Interruption.]—by severely underfunded provision. Schools that had substantial surpluses have seen that money used for ALN provision. [Interruption.] If you want to intervene, please do, and I'll try and educate you. The school system failed. [Interruption.]
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Nid wyf erioed wedi clywed pobl yn siarad mewn dadl gyda chymaint o anwybodaeth. Fe ymatebaf i un peth. Mae yna gonsortiwm prynu Cymru, lle daw awdurdodau lleol at ei gilydd i brynu pethau'n rhad rhyngddynt.

Mae llywodraeth leol yn darparu llawer o'r gwasanaethau allweddol a ddarperir gan y sector cyhoeddus yng Nghymru—nid yn unig casglu sbwriel, ond cannoedd o wasanaethau, o gynnal a chadw ffyrdd i safonau masnach. Nid oes unrhyw awdurdod lleol yn codi'r dreth gyngor oherwydd eu bod eisiau cosbi eu hetholwyr—byddai hynny'n wrthnysig ac yn hunan-drechol. Mae codiadau treth gyngor yn cael eu gyrru gan yr angen i ateb y galw, bodloni eu rhwymedigaethau statudol a dymuniadau talwyr y dreth gyngor. Rhaid inni ystyried nad ymarfer mathemategol syml yw pwysau cyllidebol ar awdurdodau lleol. Pam 4.99 y cant? Rwy'n gwybod ei fod yn gwneud pennawd da. A all Reform gyhoeddi'r cyfrifiadau sy'n sail iddo? Pa wasanaethau y byddent yn ystyried eu diddymu? A ydynt yn ceisio gwneud gwasanaethau statudol yn anstatudol er mwyn i gynghorau roi'r gorau i wasanaethau'n gyfreithlon? Yng Nghaint dan arweiniad Reform, mae cofrestr risg ariannol y gyllideb yn datgelu aramlygiad uniongyrchol o £411 miliwn—dyna ni, £411 miliwn—sy'n dangos maint yr ansicrwydd sy'n wynebu cyllid Caint. Mae'r risgiau'n cynnwys gorwariant posibl, gwasanaethau wedi'u tanariannu, pwysau galw cynyddol mewn gofal cymdeithasol, a gwaith cynnal seilwaith. Mae'r lefel hon o risg yn codi cwestiwn am allu'r cyngor i reoli ei gronfeydd wrth gefn ac osgoi toriadau mwy llym yn y blynyddoedd i ddod, gan gamblo gyda gwasanaethau i bobl agored i niwed a chyllid y cyngor.

Derbyniodd Pwyllgor Cyllid y Senedd flaenorol dystiolaeth gan dystion am y cyfraddau gwahaniaethol y mae chwyddiant yn effeithio ar eu cyllidebau. Mae gan lywodraeth leol yng Nghymru lawer o bwysau ariannol y tu allan i'w rheolaeth. Mae addysg yn faes gwariant mawr ac mae angen talu cyflogau athrawon a chodiadau pensiwn yn llawn. Addysg yw'r allwedd i symud plant allan o dlodi.

Rwyf am drafod tri math o bwysau ariannol mawr ar lywodraeth leol yn fanwl. Y pwysau amcangyfrifedig am wasanaethau llywodraeth leol eleni oedd £599 miliwn. Mae gwasanaethau cymdeithasol yn unig yn costio bron i hanner hynny, sy'n cyfateb i dros £200 miliwn i gyd. Mae darparu gofal cymdeithasol yn hanfodol er mwyn i'r system iechyd a gofal weithredu'n effeithiol, ac mae'n chwarae rhan allweddol yn cyflawni canlyniadau iechyd cadarnhaol. Mae buddsoddi mewn gofal cymdeithasol yn arwain yn uniongyrchol at leihau'r pwysau ar y GIG, o ran cadw pobl allan o'r ysbyty a helpu pobl i ddychwelyd adref ar yr adeg briodol, gan leihau oedi wrth drosglwyddo gofal.

Mae gan Gymru boblogaeth sy'n heneiddio ac mae pobl yn byw'n hwy gydag anghenion gofal cymhleth a dementia. Bydd hyn yn parhau i gynyddu'r pwysau ar wasanaethau gofal. Mae Cymdeithas Llywodraeth Leol Cymru yn pwysleisio bod gwasanaethau cymdeithasol yn wynebu heriau ariannol acíwt sy'n ehangu, gyda mwy na 81,000 o bobl yn dibynnu ar ofal a chymorth. Mae Fforwm Gofal Cymru yn dweud bod y sector o dan straen enfawr, yn ymdopi â phwysau gweithlu parhaus, cyfraddau ffioedd anghynaliadwy a chostau cynyddol cyflogwyr. Dangoswyd i bwyllgor y gall ffioedd am ofal nyrsio amrywio cymaint â £9,000 y flwyddyn rhwng awdurdodau cyfagos. I'r rhai sy'n ariannu eu gofal eu hunain yn llawn, mae costau wythnosol cyfartalog oddeutu £1,156 ar gyfer gofal preswyl a £1,394 ar gyfer gofal nyrsio. Mae'r comisiynydd pobl hŷn yn nodi sut y mae pwysau ariannu'n disgyn yn annheg ar ddefnyddwyr gwasanaeth, gyda strwythurau ffioedd annheg a ffioedd ychwanegol yn gadael llawer o'r rhai sy'n ariannu eu gofal eu hunain yn rhoi cymhorthdal i leoliadau cartrefi gofal a ariennir yn gyhoeddus i bob pwrpas.

Pwysau'r gweithlu: mae pwysau staffio'n parhau i fod yn bryder mawr, gyda swyddi gwag cronig ac anawsterau recriwtio a chadw staff parhaus, er gwaethaf cyflwyno'r cyflog byw gwirioneddol i weithwyr gofal cymdeithasol. Mae mwy na chwarter y gweithwyr gofal cartref ar gontractau dim oriau. Canfu arolwg Gofal Cymdeithasol Cymru o'r gweithlu yn 2025 fod un o bob pump o weithwyr gofal cymdeithasol yn anelu at adael y sector o fewn y 14 mis nesaf, gan nodi cyflog isel, amodau gwael a chyfleoedd cyfyngedig i gamu ymlaen fel rhesymau.

Nid yw Llywodraeth Cymru'n cyhoeddi data ar amseroedd aros am wasanaethau gofal cymdeithasol ar hyn o bryd, ond mae rhanddeiliaid yn adrodd am oedi hir a chynyddol, gan gynnwys aros am asesiad i gael pecynnau gofal, offer a therapi galwedigaethol. Canfu ymchwil Age Cymru fod bron i un o bob pedwar o bobl hŷn yn aros mwy na 30 diwrnod am asesiad gofal ac un o bob chwech yn aros mwy na 30 diwrnod i ofal gael ei roi ar waith ar ôl yr asesiad.

Maes arall lle ceir pwysau mawr yw anghenion dysgu ychwanegol. Rydym wedi siarad llawer amdano yma, ac roedd pawb yn dweud sut y mae angen mwy o arian arnom ar gyfer anghenion dysgu ychwanegol. O ble rydych chi'n meddwl y daw? Mae ysgolion ledled Cymru ar ymyl y dibyn. Mae nifer sylweddol o gyllidebau ysgolion mewn diffyg ar hyn o bryd, ac i lawer, mae'r argyfwng hwnnw'n cael ei yrru bron yn uniongyrchol—[Torri ar draws.]—gan ddarpariaeth wedi'i thanariannu'n ddifrifol. Mae ysgolion sydd ag arian sylweddol dros ben wedi gweld yr arian hwnnw'n cael ei ddefnyddio ar gyfer y ddarpariaeth ADY. [Torri ar draws.] Os ydych chi eisiau ymyrryd, gwnewch hynny os gwelwch yn dda, ac fe geisiaf eich addysgu chi. Fe fethodd y system ysgolion. [Torri ar draws.]

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Reform UK: Refferenda lleol ar gyfer codiadau'r dreth gyngor
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Diolch, Lywydd. Cor blimey, I'm on my hobby horse now, I'm afraid. Now, this may shock some, but I have to begin by congratulating Reform. [Interruption.] Not because you've come up with a brilliant idea of a new policy, but because once again you've demonstrated an impressive talent for taking good Conservative ideas and applying the Reform logo to them. Now, as they say, imitation is the sincerest form of flattery. But let's just remind people in this Chamber who weren't here years ago—. I'll just remind you that you did that, of course, with your pre-election manifesto launch, which was a direct copy-and-paste job of good Conservative policies.

Now then, it was a Welsh Conservative manifesto pledge to fix council tax, and has always been a solid manifesto pledge not only to fix council tax, but to reduce council tax. Indeed, it was the Conservatives who have long noted the importance of low council tax, and, in 2011, I was proud to have been elected here when the Right Honourable David Cameron, Conservative Prime Minister, actually provided a three years' council tax freeze—£50 million—to the Welsh Government, Labour propped up by Plaid Cymru. But guess what, folks? They did not pass those moneys on to secure reductions in council tax, instead spending it on their own pet projects.

We as a party, we fight to keep all taxes low. It is the solid foundation of the Conservative Party to allow those who work hard, and our cash-strapped pensioners, to have more money in their pockets, not just at the end of the week or the end of the month, but day in, day out. Now, we have long advocated—. And I can name the Secretaries, Cabinet Secretaries, Ministers that have been in post here—there isn't one that we haven't raised with, on these benches, the idea of a 5 per cent cap on council tax increases. If you look at our own local authority in Conwy, over the past three years nigh on 10 per cent—9.8 per cent; 9.6 per cent—and people are getting less. We've got more weeds than ever before, toilets closing down, we've got litter on our streets, and people genuinely wonder what on earth they pay their council tax for.

Now, this system already exists in England, where referendums are required for what Government determines to be excessive council tax increases. The principle has been established for more than a decade and it does provide an important democratic safeguard. What is perhaps most remarkable is hearing this proposal from Reform, a party whose own councils in England have discovered that campaigning against tax rises is rather easier than governing in those councils. So, you say one thing before an election—. And this is pre-local government election talk and spin. [Interruption.] No, we mean it, every day. It's not a come-day, go-day. We believe that there should be a referendum on council tax. And, of course, we've made these same arguments for years; long before you were ever a twinkle in Nigel Farage's eye. [Laughter.]

Across Wales, residents are facing average council tax rises—average—of 7.2 per cent. But, as I've mentioned, there are others who have the audacity to try getting 10 per cent. Now, after 26—actually, it's 27 now—years of a Welsh Labour Government, propped up by Plaid Cymru, the council tax system in Wales is broken. [Interruption.] Yes. From you, Sarah, any day; yes.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Diolch, Lywydd. Mawredd, rwy'n canu fy hoff gân nawr, mae arnaf ofn. Nawr, efallai y bydd hyn yn sioc i rai, ond rhaid imi ddechrau trwy longyfarch Reform. [Torri ar draws.] Nid oherwydd eich bod wedi dod o hyd i syniad gwych am bolisi newydd, ond oherwydd eich bod chi unwaith eto wedi dangos talent drawiadol i gymryd syniadau Ceidwadol da a gosod logo Reform arnynt. Nawr, fel maent yn dweud, dynwared yw'r ffurf fwyaf diffuant ar ganmoliaeth. Ond gadewch inni atgoffa pobl yn y Siambr hon nad oedd yma flynyddoedd yn ôl—. Fe wnaf eich atgoffa eich bod wedi gwneud hynny wrth lansio eich maniffesto cyn yr etholiad, a chopïo a gludo polisïau Ceidwadol da yn uniongyrchol.

Nawr, roedd yn addewid maniffesto gan y Ceidwadwyr Cymreig i drwsio treth gyngor, ac mae bob amser wedi bod yn addewid maniffesto cadarn nid yn unig i drwsio treth gyngor, ond i leihau'r dreth gyngor. Yn wir, y Ceidwadwyr sydd ers amser maith wedi nodi pwysigrwydd treth gyngor isel, ac yn 2011, roeddwn yn falch o gael fy ethol yma pan wnaeth y Gwir Anrhydeddus David Cameron, y Prif Weinidog Ceidwadol, rewi'r dreth gyngor am dair blynedd—£50 miliwn—i Lywodraeth Cymru, sef Llafur wedi'i chynnal gan Blaid Cymru. Ond dyfalwch beth? Ni wnaethant drosglwyddo'r arian hwnnw yn ei flaen i sicrhau gostyngiadau yn y dreth gyngor, gan ei wario yn lle hynny ar eu hoff brosiectau eu hunain.

Rydym ni fel plaid yn ymladd i gadw'r holl drethi'n isel. Sylfaen gadarn i'r Blaid Geidwadol yw caniatáu i'r rhai sy'n gweithio'n galed, a'n pensiynwyr sy'n brin o arian parod, gael mwy o arian yn eu pocedi, nid ar ddiwedd yr wythnos neu ddiwedd y mis yn unig, ond o un diwrnod i'r llall. Nawr, ers amser maith rydym wedi cefnogi—. A gallaf enwi'r Ysgrifenyddion, Ysgrifenyddion y Cabinet, Gweinidogion sydd wedi bod yn eu swyddi yma—nid oes un nad ydym ni ar y meinciau hyn wedi codi'r syniad gyda nhw o gap o 5 y cant ar godiadau i'r dreth gyngor. Os edrychwch ar ein hawdurdod lleol ni yng Nghonwy, dros y tair blynedd diwethaf bron i 10 y cant—9.8 y cant; 9.6 y cant—ac mae pobl yn cael llai. Mae gennym fwy o chwyn nag erioed o'r blaen, toiledau'n cau, mae gennym sbwriel ar ein strydoedd, ac mae pobl yn meddwl o ddifrif beth ar y ddaear y maent yn talu amdano drwy eu treth gyngor.

Nawr, mae'r system hon eisoes yn bodoli yn Lloegr, lle mae angen refferenda ar gyfer yr hyn y mae'r Llywodraeth yn penderfynu ei fod yn gynnydd gormodol yn y dreth gyngor. Mae'r egwyddor wedi'i sefydlu ers dros ddegawd ac mae'n darparu mesur diogelwch democrataidd pwysig. Yr hyn sydd efallai'n fwyaf rhyfeddol yw clywed y cynnig hwn gan Reform, plaid y mae ei chynghorau eu hunain yn Lloegr wedi darganfod bod ymgyrchu yn erbyn codiadau treth yn haws na llywodraethu yn y cynghorau hynny. Felly, rydych chi'n dweud un peth cyn etholiad—. A siarad sbin cyn etholiadau llywodraeth leol yw hyn. [Torri ar draws.] Na, rydym ni'n ei olygu, bob dydd. Nid ydym yn chwit-chwat. Rydym ni'n credu y dylai fod refferendwm ar y dreth gyngor. Ac wrth gwrs, rydym wedi gwneud y dadleuon hyn ers blynyddoedd; ymhell cyn i chi fod yn belydryn yn llygad Nigel Farage. [Chwerthin.]

Ledled Cymru, mae trigolion yn wynebu codiadau cyfartalog yn y dreth gyngor—cyfartaledd—o 7.2 y cant. Ond fel y dywedais, mae yna eraill sydd â'r hyfdra i geisio cael 10 y cant. Nawr, ar ôl 26—mae'n 27 bellach—o Lywodraeth Lafur Cymru, wedi'i chynnal gan Blaid Cymru, mae'r system dreth gyngor yng Nghymru wedi torri. [Torri ar draws.] Iawn. Gennych chi, Sarah, unrhyw bryd; iawn.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Reform UK: Refferenda lleol ar gyfer codiadau'r dreth gyngor
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Sarah, you are right to point out that Reform say one thing and do another. Now—[Interruption.] The figures, I won't repeat them again, but—. A £600-plus increase in the average band D council tax bill in Wales over the past five years. The annual band D council tax bill in Conwy County Borough Council being £2,472 and in Kensington and Chelsea, £1,643. How can that be right?

After more than two decades of Labour-led Government, with Plaid Cymru support, residents are paying more, but are not necessarily seeing improvements in services they deliver. I would ask, Cabinet Secretary, please have a look at ensuring that referendums are brought into Wales for council tax increases of 5 per cent or more. I think that way it would be very fair for our residents, our hard-working families, and, indeed, our cash-strapped pensioners. Diolch.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Sarah, rydych chi'n iawn i nodi bod Reform yn dweud un peth ac yn gwneud rhywbeth arall. Nawr—[Torri ar draws.] Y ffigurau, nid wyf am hailadrodd eto, ond—. Cynnydd o £600 a mwy yn y bil treth gyngor band D cyfartalog yng Nghymru dros y pum mlynedd diwethaf. Bil blynyddol y dreth gyngor band D yng Nghyngor Bwrdeistref Sirol Conwy oedd £2,472 ac yn Kensington a Chelsea, £1,643. Sut y gall hynny fod yn iawn?

Ar ôl mwy na dau ddegawd o Lywodraeth dan arweiniad Llafur, gyda chefnogaeth Plaid Cymru, mae trigolion yn talu mwy, ond nid ydynt o reidrwydd yn gweld gwelliannau yn y gwasanaethau y maent yn eu darparu. Hoffwn ofyn i chi edrych, Ysgrifennydd y Cabinet, ar sicrhau bod refferenda'n cael eu cyflwyno yng Nghymru ar gyfer codiadau yn y dreth gyngor o 5 y cant neu fwy. Rwy'n credu y byddai hynny'n deg iawn i'n trigolion, ein teuluoedd gweithgar, a'n pensiynwyr sy'n brin o arian parod. Diolch.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Reform UK: Refferenda lleol ar gyfer codiadau'r dreth gyngor
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Before I start—. Mike, I've got to take the bait. You talk of ignorance; we are standing up for taxpayers. Ignorance is your party sitting on its hands for 27 years and doing nothing but cripple our local government. So, let's start—[Interruption.] Yes, of course.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: Cyn i mi ddechrau—. Mike, rhaid imi fachu'r abwyd. Rydych chi'n sôn am anwybodaeth; rydym ni'n sefyll dros drethdalwyr. Anwybodaeth yw eich plaid chi'n eistedd ar ei dwylo am 27 mlynedd ac yn gwneud dim ond parlysu ein llywodraeth leol. Felly, gadewch inni ddechrau—[Torri ar draws.] Iawn, wrth gwrs.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Reform UK: Refferenda lleol ar gyfer codiadau'r dreth gyngor
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Do you want to go around telling elderly people they can't have home care support because you want to save money?
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: A ydych chi eisiau mynd o gwmpas yn dweud wrth bobl oedrannus na allant gael cymorth gofal cartref am eich bod chi eisiau arbed arian?

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Reform UK: Refferenda lleol ar gyfer codiadau'r dreth gyngor
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Twenty-seven years of failure. We're putting taxpayers first, Mike, that's what we're doing. And this is an incredibly effective tool. We've already seen it work in England. [Interruption.] Not a single local authority dares go to the electorate this year in England because they recognise that people are under enough financial pressure. Unsurprisingly, these rules have already made careful financial management in local authorities the preferred option, compared to simply asking residents to pay evermore taxes. Inflation-busting tax rises are no longer the default option in England. Currently, these protections offered to English taxpayers are not afforded to Welsh taxpayers.

Our residents in Wales are paying more than average. Over the last decade, residents in Denbighshire have seen their council tax rise by 61.9 per cent; in Flintshire, 75 per cent; Wrexham, 76 per cent; and in Conwy, 84 per cent, in a decade. The inflation rate over the same period was 34 per cent. Despite those excessive increases, this financial year, all of those local authorities increased council tax by above inflation again. And this pattern is set to continue because our local authorities are fighting with their hands tied behind their backs.

As my colleague Cai Parry-Jones has highlighted, we need council mergers. Welsh Labour was wrong to reject the offer made by Conwy and Denbighshire to merge; stopping a proposal that could have seen savings of over £1 million on middle and front-line services, over £2 million on back-office functions and the creation of a single management team that could have saved thousands.

Then we come to the funding formula. We are told that data is fundamental in driving budget allocations through the revenue support grant. But, again, local authorities are being failed in Wales. The formula uses data, Members, that is older than me. It comes from the 1991 census. Unsurprisingly, the WLGA have explained that calls from local authorities have grown for a thorough independent external review to be undertaken. I agree, and we need to see the Government get on and do this, and bring forward the proposals for the formula change urgently.

But why make this change now? There needs to be a wake-up call in this Chamber, Members, about the level of debt that local authorities are carrying. Conwy council has around £230 million of debt; Flintshire, £360 million; and Wrexham over £0.5 billion in debt. This situation is only going to get worse. From my time as a county councillor, I know that when these loans are taken, they are assumed—[Interruption.] I'll take a second intervention.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Saith mlynedd ar hugain o fethiant. Rydym ni'n rhoi trethdalwyr yn gyntaf, Mike, dyna beth rydym ni'n ei wneud. Ac mae hwn yn offeryn hynod effeithiol. Rydym eisoes wedi ei weld yn gweithio yn Lloegr. [Torri ar draws.] Nid oes unrhyw awdurdod lleol yn meiddio troi at yr etholwyr eleni yn Lloegr am eu bod yn cydnabod bod pobl o dan ddigon o bwysau ariannol. Nid yw'n syndod, mae'r rheolau hyn eisoes wedi gwneud rheolaeth ariannol ofalus mewn awdurdodau lleol yn opsiwn a ffafrir, o'i gymharu â gofyn i drigolion dalu mwyfwy o drethi. Nid yw codiadau treth sy'n uwch na chwyddiant bellach yn opsiwn diofyn yn Lloegr. Ar hyn o bryd, nid yw'r mesurau diogelwch a gynigir i drethdalwyr Lloegr yn cael eu rhoi i drethdalwyr Cymru.

Mae ein trigolion yng Nghymru yn talu mwy na'r cyfartaledd. Dros y degawd diwethaf, mae trigolion sir Ddinbych wedi gweld eu treth gyngor yn codi 61.9 y cant; yn sir y Fflint, 75 y cant; Wrecsam, 76 y cant; ac yng Nghonwy, 84 y cant, mewn degawd. Y gyfradd chwyddiant dros yr un cyfnod oedd 34 y cant. Er gwaethaf y codiadau gormodol hynny, y flwyddyn ariannol hon, cynyddodd pob un o'r awdurdodau lleol hynny eu treth gyngor uwchlaw chwyddiant eto. Ac mae'r patrwm hwn ar fin parhau am fod ein hawdurdodau lleol yn ymladd gyda'u dwylo wedi'u clymu y tu ôl i'w cefnau.

Fel y mae fy nghyd-Aelod Cai Parry-Jones wedi nodi, mae angen uno cynghorau. Roedd Llafur Cymru yn anghywir i wrthod y cynnig a wnaed gan Gonwy a sir Ddinbych i uno; rhwystrodd gynnig a allai fod wedi gweld arbedion o dros £1 filiwn ar wasanaethau rheng ganol a rheng flaen, dros £2 filiwn ar swyddogaethau swyddfa gefn a chreu un tîm rheoli a allai fod wedi arbed miloedd.

Yna down at y fformiwla ariannu. Dywedir wrthym fod data'n hanfodol i yrru dyraniadau cyllideb drwy'r grant cymorth refeniw. Ond unwaith eto, mae awdurdodau lleol yn cael cam yng Nghymru. Mae'r fformiwla'n defnyddio data, Aelodau, sy'n hŷn na fi. Daw o gyfrifiad 1991. Nid yw'n syndod fod CLlLC wedi esbonio bod galwadau gan awdurdodau lleol wedi tyfu am gynnal adolygiad allanol annibynnol trylwyr. Rwy'n cytuno, ac mae angen inni weld y Llywodraeth yn bwrw ymlaen i wneud hyn, a chyflwyno'r cynigion ar gyfer newid y fformiwla ar frys.

Ond pam gwneud y newid hwn nawr? Aelodau, mae angen i'r Siambr hon fod yn ymwybodol o lefel y ddyled y mae awdurdodau lleol yn ei chario. Mae gan gyngor Conwy tua £230 miliwn o ddyled; sir y Fflint, £360 miliwn; a Wrecsam dros £0.5 biliwn o ddyled. Mae'r sefyllfa hon yn mynd i waethygu. O fy amser fel cynghorydd sir, rwy'n gwybod pan gymerir y benthyciadau hyn, y rhagdybir eu bod—[Torri ar draws.] Fe dderbyniaf ail ymyriad.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Reform UK: Refferenda lleol ar gyfer codiadau'r dreth gyngor
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: What about public services? How do you pay for them?
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: Beth am wasanaethau cyhoeddus? Sut ydych chi'n talu am y rheini?

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Reform UK: Refferenda lleol ar gyfer codiadau'r dreth gyngor
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
The situation is getting worse. Councils borrow the debt on repayment terms expected to be 10, 15 or 20 years or more, but the repayment periods are only, often, five years. So, this means that when the loans mature, new deals need to be made and, with current interest rates, they're often much higher than originally forecast, meaning financing often falls to local authorities to find the extra money to continue to finance these debts. These debts are a ticking financial time bomb. 

The solution is not more excessive council tax rises, which is the option that many local authorities will turn to, not more reliance on borrowing, not the decline in offers for mergers. It is not continuing a funding formula system based on data that is older than me. The solution is fundamental reform of local government in Wales. That must start with greater protection for our taxpayers. Council tax referenda will do just that. They will raise awareness of the serious state of our local government finance, they will challenge the cabinet and officers to work in a more effective way, and give voters the final say on the financial direction of their local area. Members, I urge you to support this motion.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Mae'r sefyllfa'n gwaethygu. Mae cynghorau'n benthyca'r ddyled ar delerau ad-dalu y disgwylir iddynt fod yn 10, 15 neu 20 mlynedd neu fwy, ond dim ond pum mlynedd yw'r cyfnodau ad-dalu yn aml. Felly, mae hyn yn golygu, pan fydd y benthyciadau'n aeddfedu, mae angen gwneud cytundebau newydd a chyda chyfraddau llog cyfredol, maent yn aml yn llawer uwch na'r hyn a ragwelwyd yn wreiddiol, sy'n golygu bod cyllido'n aml yn golygu bod angen i awdurdodau lleol ddod o hyd i arian ychwanegol i barhau i ariannu'r dyledion hyn. Bomiau amser ariannol yw'r dyledion hyn.

Nid rhagor o godiadau treth gyngor gormodol yw'r ateb, er mai dyna'r opsiwn y bydd llawer o awdurdodau lleol yn troi ato, nid mwy o ddibyniaeth ar fenthyca, nid y gostyngiad yn nifer y cynigion ar gyfer uno. Nid parhau â system fformiwla ariannu sy'n seiliedig ar ddata sy'n hŷn na fi. Yr ateb yw diwygio llywodraeth leol yng Nghymru yn sylfaenol. Rhaid i hynny ddechrau gyda mwy o ddiogelwch i'n trethdalwyr. Bydd refferenda treth gyngor yn gwneud hynny. Byddant yn codi ymwybyddiaeth o gyflwr difrifol ein cyllid llywodraeth leol, byddant yn herio'r cabinet a'r swyddogion i weithio mewn ffordd fwy effeithiol, ac yn rhoi'r gair olaf i bleidleiswyr ar gyfeiriad ariannol eu hardal leol. Aelodau, rwy'n eich annog i gefnogi'r cynnig hwn.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Reform UK: Refferenda lleol ar gyfer codiadau'r dreth gyngor
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
I think we all know that communities are really struggling in the middle of a cost-of-living crisis, and, of course, nobody wants to pay more council tax, especially in these circumstances, and the pressures that are on people at the moment are very real. We recognise that, and that's why this Plaid Cymru Government has prioritised supporting our communities by extending free school meals, expanding free childcare and cutting business rates by 30 per cent for thousands of businesses across the country.

But we also have to recognise, as others have said, that county councils deliver essential services that people rely on every single day, from social care and children's services to schools, highways and waste collections, and those services cost money to run. I was a county councillor in Wrexham for almost 20 years, so I've seen first-hand how difficult budget decisions can be, and I know many of us here understand that reality.

I can assure Reform that no county councillor wants to increase council tax, but councils have statutory responsibilities. They have to protect vulnerable children, care for older people, and maintain essential services. And let's remember that councils have had to deal with the consequences of austerity for the last 16 years, as well as rising demand and also increasing costs. And why 4.99 per cent? What happens if the cost of delivering statutory services rises by more than that? What happens if a referendum rejects the increase needed to maintain those services? Which services would Reform cut? Would it be social care, children's services, support for people with disabilities? Because those are the difficult questions Reform have to answer.

And let's look at Reform's own record across the border as well. Every major council controlled by Reform in England with responsibility for services like education and social care increased council tax this year. When Reform ran Worcestershire County Council, you increased council tax by almost 9 per cent. There wasn't a referendum. So, why is it acceptable for Reform councillors in England to raise council tax by 9 per cent without a referendum, while you're demanding that councils here in Wales face a referendum for anything above 4.99 per cent?

There's a wider point about local democracy here as well. We already elect councillors to make these decisions on behalf of our communities. And in just a few months' time, people right across Wales are going to have the opportunity to hold those councillors to account at the ballot box. Now, of course councils should be challenged, they should be transparent about their budgets, they should explain why increases are necessary, and they should consult meaningfully with residents about their priorities. But we should also recognise that every council faces different pressures, different levels of need, and different financial circumstances.

So, it might sound simple to draw a line at 4.99 per cent, but running a council isn't that simple, as Reform's own councillors in England have found out. Despite promising to root out waste, the reality is there isn't some vast army of diversity officers whose salaries can fund our schools and social care. And when you're responsible for delivering services and protecting the most vulnerable, you can't just ignore the financial realities. And I think the people of Wales deserve to know what Reform's proposals would mean in practice, which services—.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Rwy'n credu ein bod ni i gyd yn gwybod bod cymunedau'n cael trafferth yng nghanol argyfwng costau byw, ac wrth gwrs, nid oes neb eisiau talu mwy o dreth gyngor, yn enwedig yn yr amgylchiadau hyn, ac mae'r pwysau sydd ar bobl ar hyn o bryd yn real iawn. Rydym yn cydnabod hynny, a dyna pam y mae Llywodraeth Plaid Cymru wedi blaenoriaethu cefnogi ein cymunedau drwy ehangu prydau ysgol am ddim, ehangu gofal plant am ddim a lleihau ardrethi busnes 30 y cant i filoedd o fusnesau ledled y wlad.

Ond rhaid inni hefyd gydnabod, fel y mae eraill wedi dweud, fod cynghorau sir yn darparu gwasanaethau hanfodol y mae pobl yn dibynnu arnynt bob dydd, o ofal cymdeithasol a gwasanaethau plant i ysgolion, priffyrdd a chasgliadau gwastraff, ac mae'r gwasanaethau hynny'n costio arian i'w rhedeg. Roeddwn i'n gynghorydd sir yn Wrecsam am bron i 20 mlynedd, felly fe welais drosof fy hun pa mor anodd y gall penderfyniadau cyllidebol fod, ac rwy'n gwybod bod llawer ohonom yma yn deall y gwirionedd hwnnw.

Gallaf sicrhau Reform nad oes unrhyw gynghorydd sir eisiau cynyddu'r dreth gyngor, ond mae gan gynghorau gyfrifoldebau statudol. Rhaid iddynt ddiogelu plant agored i niwed, gofalu am bobl hŷn, a chynnal gwasanaethau hanfodol. A gadewch inni gofio bod cynghorau wedi gorfod delio â chanlyniadau cyni am y 16 mlynedd diwethaf, yn ogystal â galw a chostau cynyddol. A pham 4.99 y cant? Beth sy'n digwydd os bydd cost darparu gwasanaethau statudol yn codi mwy na hynny? Beth sy'n digwydd os yw refferendwm yn gwrthod y cynnydd sydd ei angen i gynnal y gwasanaethau hynny? Pa wasanaethau fyddai Reform yn eu torri? Ai gofal cymdeithasol, gwasanaethau plant, cymorth i bobl ag anableddau? Oherwydd dyna'r cwestiynau anodd y mae'n rhaid i Reform eu hateb.

A gadewch inni edrych ar hanes Reform ei hun dros y ffin hefyd. Mae pob cyngor mawr a reolir gan Reform yn Lloegr gyda chyfrifoldeb am wasanaethau fel addysg a gofal cymdeithasol wedi cynyddu'r dreth gyngor eleni. Pan oedd Reform yn rhedeg Cyngor Swydd Gaerwrangon, fe wnaethoch chi gynyddu'r dreth gyngor bron i 9 y cant. Ni chafwyd refferendwm. Felly, pam y mae'n dderbyniol i gynghorwyr Reform yn Lloegr godi'r dreth gyngor 9 y cant heb refferendwm, tra eich bod chi'n mynnu bod cynghorau yma yng Nghymru yn wynebu refferendwm ar gyfer unrhyw beth uwchlaw 4.99 y cant?

Mae pwynt ehangach am ddemocratiaeth leol yma hefyd. Rydym eisoes yn ethol cynghorwyr i wneud y penderfyniadau hyn ar ran ein cymunedau. Ac ymhen ychydig fisoedd, bydd pobl ledled Cymru yn cael cyfle i ddwyn y cynghorwyr hynny i gyfrif yn y blwch pleidleisio. Nawr, wrth gwrs y dylid herio cynghorau, dylent fod yn dryloyw ynglŷn â'u cyllidebau, dylent esbonio pam y mae angen cynnydd, a dylent ymgynghori'n ystyrlon â thrigolion ynglŷn â'u blaenoriaethau. Ond dylem hefyd gydnabod bod pob cyngor yn wynebu gwahanol fathau o bwysau, gwahanol lefelau o angen, ac amgylchiadau ariannol gwahanol.

Felly, efallai fod tynnu llinell ar 4.99 y cant yn swnio'n syml, ond nid yw rhedeg cyngor mor syml â hynny, fel y mae cynghorwyr Reform eu hunain yn Lloegr wedi darganfod. Er addo cael gwared ar wastraff, y gwir amdani yw nad oes yna fyddin enfawr o swyddogion amrywiaeth y gall eu cyflogau ariannu ein hysgolion a'n gofal cymdeithasol. A phan fyddwch chi'n gyfrifol am ddarparu gwasanaethau a diogelu'r rhai mwyaf agored i niwed, ni allwch anwybyddu'r realiti ariannol. Ac rwy'n credu bod pobl Cymru yn haeddu gwybod beth fyddai cynigion Reform yn ei olygu yn ymarferol, pa wasanaethau—.

I took your intervention. 

Councillors have to make difficult decisions, but that's how local democracy works. That's what accountability means. Political leadership isn't just about the promises you make. It's about being responsible for the consequences of your decisions. And the consequences of what Reform are proposing here today could be very, very serious for our councils delivering essential services, and, importantly, for the communities who rely on them.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Fe dderbyniais eich ymyriad.

Rhaid i gynghorwyr wneud penderfyniadau anodd, ond dyna sut y mae democratiaeth leol yn gweithio. Dyna beth y mae atebolrwydd yn ei olygu. Mae arweinyddiaeth wleidyddol yn ymwneud â mwy na'r addewidion a wnewch. Mae'n ymwneud â bod yn gyfrifol am ganlyniadau eich penderfyniadau. A gallai canlyniadau'r hyn y mae Reform yn ei gynnig yma heddiw fod yn ddifrifol iawn i'n cynghorau sy'n darparu gwasanaethau hanfodol, ac yn bwysig, i'r cymunedau sy'n dibynnu arnynt.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Reform UK: Refferenda lleol ar gyfer codiadau'r dreth gyngor
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Well, we all get that brown envelope, don't we, through the post, or sometimes it's an email nowadays? Council tax is not voluntary, is it? It arrives every year and households have got to find the money to pay for it. When a council wants to raise the bill by more than 4.99 per cent, Reform UK believes that the people paying for it should have the final say. This motion does not ban a higher increase, it simply says: make the case, publish the consequences and ask permission.

The Welsh average band D council tax rose by 7.7 per cent in 2024-25, and by a further 7.2 per cent in 2025-26. Over the last five years, council tax rises across Wales have accelerated significantly, with the Welsh average increasing 7.2 per cent in 2025-26. And nowhere is that seen more than in north-east Wales where I live. In Flintshire, the council tax increase for 2025-26 was 9.5 per cent, and in Wrexham, residents faced an increase of approximately 8.9 per cent. These rises came on top of substantial increases in previous years. Where does it stop? Yet both councils continue to face severe financial challenges in themselves.

From a Flintshire and Wrexham perspective, the situation has become increasingly difficult to manage. Both authorities are forecasting budget deficits in excess of £25 million, as pointed out by Cai. Adult social care, there are issues, demand for services, additional learning needs provision, homelessness services and expensive out-of-county placements continue to grow faster than the funding available to support them.

Councils have had to make difficult decisions for well over a decade now—I'm aware of that. Flintshire and Wrexham have delivered millions of pounds of expenditure reductions since about 2010, but there comes a point where efficiencies are exhausted and residents are simply asked to pay more to cover a growing funding gap.

Before Flintshire approved its recent budget, residents were consulted. Many expressed concern about the rising council tax increases to bridge budget shortfalls during the continuing cost-of-living crisis. Despite these concerns, local people had no binding vote on the outcome—no binding vote, and that's important. When you speak to residents across Flintshire and Wrexham, you hear a common message: council tax keeps rising, but many people believe services are being reduced.

I've seen it myself. Your bins—they don't get emptied every week now. There are all sorts of places where we're seeing things cut. Potholes in the road, local road infrastructure—there are loads of issues. Whether every criticism is justified or not, the perception is clear: people are paying more and feeling they are receiving less in return. That's why local democracy comes into its own. Of course, supporters of the status quo argue that local elections are sufficiently accountable. I disagree with that. A local election provides a general mandate. A referendum provides a specific mandate for an exceptional tax increase.

And, of course, we must be honest about council finances. Reserves are not a magic pot of money that can simply solve every problem. Some reserves are earmarked, yes. Some are legally committed. And some can only be used for specific purposes. Flintshire, for example, reports significant levels of usable reserves, but much of that money is allocated for identified risks and future commitments. However, transparency is absolutely essential. If councils—
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Wel, rydym i gyd yn cael yr amlen frown honno drwy'r post, onid ydym, neu weithiau mae ar ffurf e-bost y dyddiau hyn? Nid yw'r dreth gyngor yn wirfoddol. Mae'n cyrraedd bob blwyddyn ac mae'n rhaid i aelwydydd ddod o hyd i'r arian i'w thalu. Pan fydd cyngor eisiau codi'r bil fwy na 4.99 y cant, mae Reform UK yn credu y dylai'r bobl sy'n ei thalu gael y gair olaf. Nid yw'r cynnig hwn yn gwahardd cynnydd uwch, mae'n dweud yn syml: cyflwynwch yr achos, cyhoeddwch y canlyniadau a gofynnwch am ganiatâd.

Cododd treth gyngor band D yng Nghymru Cymru 7.7 y cant ar gyfartaledd yn 2024-25, a 7.2 y cant arall yn 2025-26. Dros y pum mlynedd diwethaf, mae cynnydd yn y dreth gyngor ledled Cymru wedi cyflymu'n sylweddol, gyda chyfartaledd Cymru yn cynyddu 7.2 y cant yn 2025-26. Ac nid oes unrhyw le'n dangos hynny fwy nag yng ngogledd-ddwyrain Cymru lle rwy'n byw. Yn sir y Fflint, y cynnydd yn y dreth gyngor ar gyfer 2025-26 oedd 9.5 y cant, ac yn Wrecsam, roedd trigolion yn wynebu cynnydd o oddeutu 8.9 y cant. Daeth y codiadau hyn ar ben cynnydd sylweddol yn y blynyddoedd blaenorol. Ble mae'n dod i ben? Ond mae'r ddau gyngor yn parhau i wynebu heriau ariannol difrifol eu hunain.

O safbwynt sir y Fflint a Wrecsam, mae'r sefyllfa wedi dod yn fwyfwy anodd i'w rheoli. Mae'r ddau awdurdod yn rhagweld diffygion cyllidebol o dros £25 miliwn, fel y nododd Cai. Mae materion yn codi gyda gofal cymdeithasol i oedolion, a'r galw am wasanaethau, darpariaeth anghenion dysgu ychwanegol, gwasanaethau digartrefedd a lleoliadau drud y tu allan i'r sir yn parhau i dyfu'n gyflymach na'r cyllid sydd ar gael i gefnogi'r galw hwnnw.

Mae cynghorau wedi gorfod gwneud penderfyniadau anodd ers dros ddegawd bellach—rwy'n ymwybodol o hynny. Mae sir y Fflint a Wrecsam wedi cyflawni miliynau o bunnoedd o ostyngiadau mewn gwariant ers tua 2010, ond daw pwynt lle mae arbedion effeithlonrwydd wedi eu dihysbyddu a gofynnir i drigolion dalu mwy i lenwi bwlch cyllido cynyddol.

Cyn i sir y Fflint gymeradwyo ei chyllideb ddiweddar, ymgynghorwyd â thrigolion. Mynegodd nifer bryder am y codiadau cynyddol yn y dreth gyngor i bontio diffygion cyllidebol yn ystod yr argyfwng costau byw parhaus. Er gwaethaf y pryderon hyn, nid oedd gan bobl leol unrhyw bleidlais rwymol ar y canlyniad—dim pleidlais rwymol, ac mae hynny'n bwysig. Pan siaradwch chi â thrigolion ar draws sir y Fflint a Wrecsam, rydych chi'n clywed neges gyffredin: mae'r dreth gyngor yn parhau i godi, ond mae llawer o bobl yn credu bod gwasanaethau'n cael eu lleihau.

Fe'i gwelais fy hun. Eich biniau—ni chânt eu gwagio bob wythnos nawr. Mae yna bob math o lefydd lle gwelwn bethau'n cael eu torri. Tyllau yn y ffordd, seilwaith ffyrdd lleol—mae yna lwyth o broblemau. P'un a yw pob beirniadaeth yn gyfiawn ai peidio, mae'r canfyddiad yn glir: mae pobl yn talu mwy ac yn teimlo eu bod yn cael llai yn gyfnewid. Dyna pam y mae democratiaeth leol yn bwysig. Wrth gwrs, mae cefnogwyr y status quo yn dadlau bod etholiadau lleol yn ddigon atebol. Rwy'n anghytuno â hynny. Mae etholiad lleol yn darparu mandad cyffredinol. Mae refferendwm yn darparu mandad penodol ar gyfer cynnydd eithriadol i'r dreth.

Ac wrth gwrs, rhaid inni fod yn onest ynglŷn â chyllid y cyngor. Nid yw cronfeydd wrth gefn yn bot o arian gwyrthiol sy'n gallu datrys pob problem. Mae rhai cronfeydd wrth gefn wedi'u clustnodi. Mae rhai wedi'u rhwymo'n gyfreithiol. A dim ond at ddibenion penodol y gellir defnyddio rhai. Mae sir y Fflint, er enghraifft, yn nodi lefelau sylweddol o gronfeydd wrth gefn y gellir eu defnyddio, ond mae llawer o'r arian hwnnw'n cael ei ddyrannu ar gyfer risgiau a nodwyd ac ymrwymiadau yn y dyfodol. Fodd bynnag, mae tryloywder yn gwbl hanfodol. Os yw cynghorau—
